A hyperlink is a clickable element inside a digital document — such as a webpage, an email, or a PDF — that instantly takes you to another location when you click or tap on it. That "other location" could be another webpage, a different section of the same page, a file, or even your email app.

Think of it like a magic door. You're reading something on a screen, you see a door (the hyperlink), you click it, and you're immediately transported somewhere else — no searching, no typing, no effort.

A hyperlink most commonly appears as text that is underlined and colored blue, like this:

Learn more about [climate change](#)

The words "climate change" here are the hyperlink. That visible, clickable text is called the anchor text. It tells you, in plain language, where the link will take you or what it's about.

However, a hyperlink doesn't always have to be blue or underlined. Web designers can style it to look like anything — a button, a banner, a logo, or even a plain-looking word. What makes it a hyperlink isn't how it looks, but what it does: it connects you to another location when activated.

A hyperlink can also be an image. For example, clicking on a company's logo on a website often takes you to that company's homepage. The logo is the hyperlink in that case.

Every hyperlink has two parts:

  1. The visible part — what you see on the screen (the anchor text or image).
  2. The invisible part — the actual web address, formally called a URL (Uniform Resource Locator), that is embedded within it. This is the true destination. You don't see it directly on the page, but your browser reads it the moment you click.

For example, you might see the text "Click here to read the article", but hidden inside that text is a full address like https://www.example.com/articles/science/climate. When you click, your browser follows that hidden address.

You can often peek at the hidden destination by hovering your mouse cursor over the hyperlink — most browsers will show the URL at the bottom of the screen.

When you click a hyperlink, here is what happens in simple terms:

  1. Your browser reads the hidden URL stored inside the hyperlink.
  2. It sends a request to the server (a powerful computer) that hosts the content at that address.
  3. The server sends back the content.
  4. Your browser loads and displays that content — usually in the same tab, or sometimes in a new one.

All of this happens in a fraction of a second.

Not all hyperlinks work the same way. Here are the main kinds:

1. External link — Takes you to a completely different website. For example, a news article linking to a government data source.

2. Internal link — Takes you to a different page on the same website. For example, clicking "About Us" in a website's menu.

3. Anchor link (or jump link) — Takes you to a specific section of the same page you're already on, rather than loading a new page. This is common on long pages with a table of contents at the top.

4. Email link (mailto link) — Instead of opening a webpage, clicking this opens your email app with a pre-filled recipient address, ready for you to write a message.

5. File download link — Clicking this doesn't take you to a webpage; instead, it downloads a file (like a PDF, image, or video) onto your device.

Hyperlinks are everywhere in the digital world:

  • Webpages — The entire web is built on hyperlinks. Pages connect to other pages through them.
  • Emails — A link to "unsubscribe," verify your account, or read a full article.
  • Word documents and PDFs — Documents often contain clickable links to sources or references.
  • Social media posts — A link shared in a post that takes you to an article or video.
  • E-books and digital magazines — Footnotes and references that link to their sources.

Hyperlinks are the fundamental building blocks of the World Wide Web. The entire internet is essentially a massive web of documents and pages all connected to each other through hyperlinks — which is exactly why it's called a "web." Without hyperlinks, you would have to manually type every single web address to navigate anywhere online. Hyperlinks make navigation seamless, fast, and intuitive.

They also give authors a way to reference and credit other sources without copying content — a reader can simply click through to read more if they choose to.
"She clicked the hyperlink in the email, which took her directly to the company's registration page."

A hyperlink is a clickable element — usually text or an image — embedded in a digital document that navigates you to another location (a webpage, file, email, or section of the same page) when clicked. It has a visible face (what you see) and a hidden destination (the URL it carries). It is the core mechanism that connects the entire internet together.
